subtitle: Combinational logic has no memory. Feed an output back to an input and you get a circuit that remembers.

seq.body:
A calculator that forgot every number the moment you let go of the keys would be useless. So how does a circuit remember? A combinational output depends only on the present inputs. A sequential circuit’s output also depends on its state, meaning what happened before, stored in latches or flip-flops.

The simplest memory is two cross-coupled NOR (or NAND) gates: each output feeds the other’s input, so the pair holds whichever state it was last pushed into, like two people each repeating what the other said. What distinguishes a sequential circuit? Its output depends on stored state, not only on present inputs.
keynotes: A combinational output depends only on the present inputs; a sequential circuit’s output also depends on its state, stored in latches or flip-flops.
The simplest memory is two cross-coupled NOR (or NAND) gates, each output feeding the other’s input.
The pair holds whichever state it was last pushed into.

sr.body:
Meet your first memory cell, the SR latch, with two inputs: S (set) and R (reset). S = 1 forces Q = 1; R = 1 forces Q = 0; S = R = 0 holds the previous Q. And S = R = 1 is forbidden: both outputs collapse, and releasing both at once is unpredictable.

Try it yourself. Start with Q = 0. Set S = 1, R = 0 and Q becomes 1. Now return S to 0. With S = R = 0 the latch holds Q = 1: that is memory! Toggle S and R in the figure and watch Q remember. The forbidden combination is S = R = 1.
keynotes: S = 1 forces Q = 1, R = 1 forces Q = 0, and S = R = 0 holds the previous Q.
S = R = 1 is forbidden: both outputs collapse and releasing both at once is unpredictable.
Pulsing S to 1 then back to 0 leaves Q at 1: that is memory.

d.body: A latch listens all the time, which can be a problem. We want circuits to change at an exact moment, together. A D latch is transparent while the enable is high, so its output follows D. A D flip-flop is edge-triggered: it samples D only at the clock’s rising edge and holds it until the next. Edge triggering makes whole systems predictable, because every flip-flop changes at the same instant. Change D between clock edges in the figure and see that Q only follows on a rising edge.
keynotes: A D latch is transparent while the enable is high: its output follows D.
A D flip-flop is edge-triggered: it samples D only at the clock’s rising edge and holds it until the next.
Edge triggering makes whole systems predictable because every flip-flop changes at the same instant.

jkt.body:
Two more flip-flops complete the family, and their behaviour fits in a small table.

J KNext Q
0 0Q (hold)
0 10 (reset)
1 01 (set)
1 1Q′ (toggle)

The JK fixes the forbidden state by making 1,1 toggle. Tie J and K together and you get a T flip-flop: T = 1 toggles every clock, which halves the frequency. Clock a T flip-flop with T = 1 at 8 MHz: Q toggles once per clock, so one full Q cycle takes two clocks, and f_Q = 8/2 = 4 MHz. With J = K = 1, a JK flip-flop toggles.
keynotes: A JK flip-flop holds for J K = 0 0, resets for 0 1, sets for 1 0 and toggles (Q′) for 1 1.
The JK fixes the forbidden SR state by making 1,1 toggle.
A T flip-flop with T = 1 toggles every clock and halves the frequency: 8 MHz in gives 4 MHz out.

time.body:
A photographer needs the subject still while the shutter clicks. A flip-flop is the same: D must be stable for a setup time before the clock edge and a hold time after it, or the flip-flop may go metastable (neither 0 nor 1 for a while). The clock period must cover clock-to-Q delay + logic delay + setup time.

Compute a limit. With t_cq = 2 ns, logic = 8 ns and setup = 1 ns, the minimum period = 11 ns, so f_max ≈ 91 MHz. Violating setup time can cause metastability, an output stuck between 0 and 1.

tbl.body:
To design with flip-flops you need two tools, one for each direction. The characteristic equation tells you the next state: D: Q⁺ = D; T: Q⁺ = T⊕Q; JK: Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q. The excitation table runs the other way: given the wanted transition Q → Q⁺, what inputs are needed?

For JK, 0→1 needs J = 1 (K = X); 1→0 needs K = 1 (J = X). The X means “don’t care”. You will use these when designing counters and state machines. So a JK flip-flop that must go 0 → 1 needs J = 1, with K either 0 or 1.
keynotes: Characteristic equations give the next state: D: Q⁺ = D; T: Q⁺ = T⊕Q; JK: Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q.
The excitation table runs the other way: given the wanted transition Q → Q⁺, what inputs are needed?
For JK, 0→1 needs J = 1 (K = X) and 1→0 needs K = 1 (J = X).
